title: Delhi AQI Hits 511 as November Becomes Most Polluted Month on Record
excerpt: PM2.5 reached 22.1 times the WHO guideline on Sunday morning after a Saturday peak of 577; AQI.in estimates the exposure at 12.5 cigarettes a day and advises residents to stay indoors.
body:
• Delhi's AQI reached 511 on Sunday morning, November 15, in the hazardous band on AQI.in's scale, after peaking at 577 early on Saturday — November 2026 is now the most polluted month in AQI.in's record, averaging 380.
  • PM2.5 measured 331 micrograms per cubic metre, 22.1 times the WHO's annual guideline value; AQI.in estimates the exposure equals smoking 12.5 cigarettes a day, while stressing that is an exposure estimate, not the effect of actually smoking.
  • What to do: AQI.in advises avoiding outdoor exposure, wearing a mask outdoors and not exercising outside while levels stay hazardous; CPCB-based guidance adds keeping windows closed and running an air purifier indoors.
  • Delhi was far worse than other metros on Sunday: Kolkata 248, Mumbai 136, Chennai 96, Bengaluru 74.

Delhi woke on Sunday, November 15 to an air quality index of 511, in the hazardous category on AQI.in's scale, capping a weekend in which the capital's air swung violently and stayed dangerous. The index had peaked at 577 at around 7:31 a.m. on Saturday, eased to 248 by mid-afternoon, then climbed back through 400 after sunset and kept rising overnight to Sunday morning's 511, according to AQI.in data reported by Livemint. Readings on the official CPCB scale differ in method — a CPCB-data tracker put the city average at 472, still in the severe band — but both scales agree on the conclusion: Delhi's air on Sunday was at levels where health effects are expected for the entire population, not only for sensitive groups.

"Carbon monoxide stood at 1,657 parts per billion, nitrogen dioxide at 22 parts per billion and sulphur dioxide at 5 parts per billion."

What is in the air

AQI.in recorded a PM2.5 concentration of 331 micrograms per cubic metre — 22.1 times the World Health Organization's annual air quality guideline value — and PM10 at 469 micrograms per cubic metre. Carbon monoxide stood at 1,657 parts per billion, nitrogen dioxide at 22 parts per billion and sulphur dioxide at 5 parts per billion. The capital ranked 15th among the world's most polluted cities during the reported period. AQI.in estimates that breathing this air is equivalent, in exposure terms, to smoking 12.5 cigarettes a day, 87.5 a week and 375 a month — and itself cautions that these figures represent estimated exposure to pollution, not the actual effects of smoking. On health effects, AQI.in says breathing Delhi's air at these levels carries high chances of asthma, heart issues and allergies. Our earlier reporting this month covered why doctors want extra care for children's lungs this November and the outdoor workers who cannot stay inside when the air turns severe.

A record month, not a single bad day

Sunday's reading is part of a pattern rather than an isolated spike. AQI.in's pollution calendar recorded 666 on November 9 and 514 on November 12, and its annual analysis identifies November 2026 as the most polluted month in its displayed record, with an average AQI of 380. The annual average has risen from 185 in 2021 to 206 in 2025. Emergency measures were already in place before this weekend: GRAP Stage III restrictions were in force earlier this week, when the AQI stood at 321 — a level Sunday's air has far exceeded. The Livemint report carried no announcement of new measures on Sunday.

How Delhi compares, and what residents should do

No other major Indian city came close on Sunday: Kolkata recorded 248, Mumbai 136, Chennai 96 and Bengaluru 74, according to AQI.in — meaning a family deciding whether to fly a child or an elderly parent out of the capital for the week is looking at air roughly two to seven times cleaner in every other metro. While levels remain hazardous, AQI.in recommends avoiding outdoor exposure, wearing masks outdoors and refraining from exercising outside. Guidance based on CPCB bands adds the indoor half of the routine: keep windows closed, run an air purifier if you have one, and treat a well-fitting N95 as the mask standard outdoors. You can check the current station-level readings on the CPCB-data tracker for Delhi before planning any outdoor activity. For diaspora readers with parents in Delhi, the actionable version is short: this is a week to move exercise indoors, keep the purifier running, and postpone non-essential outdoor errands for elderly family members until the index falls out of the severe band.
